title: Quadratics: Formula, Completing the Square and Roots
description: Solving quadratic equations with the formula and by completing the square (including a leading coefficient), reading the discriminant, and forming a quadratic from its roots (IGCSE Extended).

notes.heading: Standard Form and the Discriminant
notes.body:
Every method in this topic starts by putting the equation in standard form and reading off three numbers.

📌 Definition
A quadratic equation in standard form is $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a \neq 0$. The **discriminant** is the expression $b^2 - 4ac$.

🔑 How it works
The discriminant tells you the nature of the roots before you solve anything:

$$b^2 - 4ac > 0 \Rightarrow \text{two distinct real roots}$$

$$b^2 - 4ac = 0 \Rightarrow \text{one repeated real root}$$

$$b^2 - 4ac < 0 \Rightarrow \text{no real roots}$$

💡 Worked Example
For $3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0$: $a = 3$, $b = -5$, $c = 2$.

Discriminant $= (-5)^2 - 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 25 - 24 = 1$, which is positive, so there are two distinct real roots.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dropping the sign of $b$. Here $b = -5$, and $b^2 = 25$ because squaring removes the minus — but in the formula the term $-b$ becomes $+5$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Move everything to one side first: $3x^2 = 5x - 2$ becomes $3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0$.
• A missing term means a zero coefficient: $x^2 - 9 = 0$ has $b = 0$.
• The discriminant is under the square root in the formula — that is why it controls the roots.

notes.heading: The Quadratic Formula
notes.body:
The formula solves any quadratic, factorisable or not.

🔑 How it works

$$x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

1. Write the equation in standard form and note $a$, $b$, $c$ with their signs.
2. Compute the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$.
3. Substitute, then take the $+$ and the $-$ separately to get both roots.

💡 Worked Example
Solve $2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0$.

Here $a = 2$, $b = 5$, $c = -3$.

Discriminant $= 5^2 - 4 \times 2 \times (-3) = 25 + 24 = 49$, and $\sqrt{49} = 7$.

$$x = \dfrac{-5 \pm 7}{4}$$

So $x = \dfrac{-5 + 7}{4} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $x = \dfrac{-5 - 7}{4} = \dfrac{-12}{4} = -3$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $-4ac$ as subtraction when $c$ is negative: $-4 \times 2 \times (-3)$ is $+24$, not $-24$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Keep the $\pm$ until the very end — it is what produces two roots.
• If the discriminant is not a perfect square, leave the answer in surd form or round only at the end.
• Check by substituting one root back into the original equation.

notes.heading: Completing the Square (Leading Coefficient 1)
notes.body:
Completing the square rewrites a quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant, which then solves itself.

🔑 How it works
The identity behind it is:

$$x^2 + bx = \left(x + \dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2$$

Halve the coefficient of $x$, square it, and subtract that square again to keep the value unchanged.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Rewrite
$x^2 + 8x + 10 = (x + 4)^2 - 16 + 10 = (x + 4)^2 - 6$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Solve
Solve $x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0$.

$(x - 3)^2 - 9 + 2 = 0$, so $(x - 3)^2 - 7 = 0$ and $(x - 3)^2 = 7$.

$x - 3 = \pm\sqrt{7}$, giving $x = 3 \pm \sqrt{7}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the subtracted square: $(x + 4)^2$ on its own expands to $x^2 + 8x + 16$, which is not the original expression.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Halve $b$ for the bracket, then subtract the square of that half.
• Solving gives a $\pm$ square root — two roots, just like the formula.
• Surd answers such as $3 \pm \sqrt{7}$ are exact and preferred in Extended.

notes.heading: Completing the Square with a Leading Coefficient
notes.body:
When $a \neq 1$, factor $a$ out of the $x$-terms before completing the square, and carry it through.

🔑 How it works

$$ax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x\right) + c = a\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - a\left(\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + c$$

In practice: factor, complete inside the bracket, then multiply the subtracted square back out by $a$.

💡 Worked Example
Write $2x^2 + 4x - 3$ in the form $a(x + p)^2 + q$.

$2x^2 + 4x - 3 = 2(x^2 + 2x) - 3 = 2\left[(x + 1)^2 - 1\right] - 3 = 2(x + 1)^2 - 2 - 3 = 2(x + 1)^2 - 5$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Solve from the form
$2(x + 1)^2 - 5 = 0$ gives $(x + 1)^2 = \dfrac{5}{2}$, so $x = -1 \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Leaving the subtracted square inside the bracket unmultiplied: the $-1$ must become $-2$ once the outer $2$ is distributed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The $a$ in front of the bracket stays in the final form $a(x + p)^2 + q$.
• Every constant inside the bracket gets multiplied by $a$ on the way out.
• If the equation side is $0$, dividing through by $a$ first is an equally valid route.

notes.heading: Reading the Discriminant
notes.body:
The discriminant answers nature-of-roots questions in one line, with no solving at all.

🔑 How it works
Compute $b^2 - 4ac$ and compare with zero. Equal (repeated) roots happen exactly when the discriminant is zero — this is how unknown-coefficient questions are solved.

💡 Worked Example 1
$x^2 + 6x + 9 = 0$: discriminant $= 36 - 36 = 0$, so there is one repeated root, $x = -3$.

💡 Worked Example 2
$x^2 + x + 1 = 0$: discriminant $= 1 - 4 = -3 < 0$, so there are no real roots. The graph never touches the $x$-axis.

💡 Worked Example 3 — Unknown coefficient
$kx^2 + 8x + 4 = 0$ has equal roots. Then $8^2 - 4 \times k \times 4 = 0$, so $64 - 16k = 0$ and $k = 4$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using $b^2 - 4ac$ with $a$, $c$ from an equation that is not in standard form. Rearrange first.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Positive: two roots. Zero: one repeated root. Negative: no real roots.
• 'Equal roots' and 'repeated root' both mean discriminant $= 0$.
• The discriminant is also the expression under the square root in the formula.

notes.heading: Forming a Quadratic from its Roots
notes.body:
Roots determine the equation, because each root $r$ contributes a factor $(x - r)$.

🔑 How it works
For roots $r_1$ and $r_2$:

$$(x - r_1)(x - r_2) = x^2 - (r_1 + r_2)x + r_1 r_2 = 0$$

Equivalently, for $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ the sum of the roots is $-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and the product is $\dfrac{c}{a}$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Roots $3$ and $-5$: sum $= -2$, product $= -15$.

Equation: $x^2 - (-2)x + (-15) = 0$, that is $x^2 + 2x - 15 = 0$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Fractional roots
Roots $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $-3$: sum $= -\dfrac{5}{2}$, product $= -\dfrac{3}{2}$.

$x^2 + \dfrac{5}{2}x - \dfrac{3}{2} = 0$, and doubling every term clears the fractions: $2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Sign slips in the sum: the middle term is MINUS the sum of the roots, so roots $3$ and $-5$ give $+2x$, not $-2x$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Factor route and sum-product route must agree — use one to check the other.
• Any non-zero multiple of the equation has the same roots; integer coefficients are the usual form.
• Sum of roots $= -b/a$, product $= c/a$ also reads roots off a given equation.

notes.heading: Choosing a Method, and Final Checks
notes.body:
Extended papers reward picking the fastest valid route and checking the answer costs nothing.

🔑 How it works
• 'Solve' with nice numbers: factorise if obvious, otherwise the formula.
• 'Solve, giving answers in surd form' or 'exact': completing the square or the formula, left unrounded.
• 'Write in the form $a(x+p)^2 + q$' or 'find the minimum point': completing the square.
• 'Nature of the roots' or 'equal roots': discriminant only.
• 'Find the equation with these roots': sum and product.

💡 Worked Example
Solve $x^2 + 4x + 1 = 0$ exactly.

Discriminant $= 16 - 4 = 12$, so $\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt{3}$ and

$$x = \dfrac{-4 \pm 2\sqrt{3}}{2} = -2 \pm \sqrt{3}$$

✅ Check
Sum of the roots $(-2 + \sqrt{3}) + (-2 - \sqrt{3}) = -4 = -b/a$, and their product $= 4 - 3 = 1 = c/a$. Both match, so the roots are right.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Rounding surd answers when the question says exact, or simplifying $\sqrt{12}$ to $\sqrt{12}$ instead of $2\sqrt{3}$ and losing the final mark.

flashcards.definition: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to 0.
flashcards.example: 3x^2 = 5x - 2 rearranges to 3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0, so a = 3, b = -5, c = 2.

flashcards.definition: The expression b^2 - 4ac; it decides how many real roots a quadratic has.
flashcards.example: For 3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0 the discriminant is 25 - 24 = 1, so two distinct real roots.

flashcards.definition: Exactly one repeated real root; also the condition for 'equal roots' questions.
flashcards.example: x^2 + 6x + 9 = 0 has discriminant 0 and the repeated root x = -3.

flashcards.definition: No real roots; the graph never crosses the x-axis.
flashcards.example: x^2 + x + 1 = 0 has discriminant 1 - 4 = -3, so no real roots.

flashcards.definition: x^2 + bx = (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2: halve the x-coefficient, then subtract its square.

flashcards.term: Completing the square with a leading coefficient
flashcards.definition: Factor a out of the x-terms first, complete inside the bracket, then multiply the subtracted square back out by a.
For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 the roots add to -b/a.
For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 the roots multiply to c/a.
x^2 - (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0, or multiply the factors (x - r1)(x - r2).
When the discriminant is not a perfect square, leave roots with the square root sign instead of rounding.
The +/- in the formula (and when square-rooting both sides) is what produces the two roots; dropping it loses one.

questions.stem: In the equation $3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0$, what are the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$?
questions.explanation: Read straight off standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, keeping signs: the x-term is -5x, so b = -5.
b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 4 x 1 x 9 = 36 - 36 = 0, which means one repeated root.

questions.stem: A quadratic has discriminant $-7$. How many real roots does it have?
questions.explanation: A negative discriminant means the square root in the formula is of a negative number, so there are no real roots.
x^2 = 9, and taking the square root gives both x = 3 and x = -3 because both square to 9.
Discriminant = 25 - 16 = 9, so x = (-5 +/- 3)/2, giving x = -1 and x = -4.
Discriminant = 49 - 24 = 25, so x = (7 +/- 5)/6, giving x = 12/6 = 2 and x = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.stem: Write $x^2 + 8x + 10$ in the form $(x + p)^2 + q$.
questions.explanation: Halve 8 to get 4, square it to get 16, then x^2 + 8x + 10 = (x + 4)^2 - 16 + 10 = (x + 4)^2 - 6.

questions.stem: Solve $x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0$ by completing the square, giving answers in surd form.

questions.explanation: Sum of roots = -5 and product = -14, so the equation is x^2 - (-5)x + (-14) = 0, that is x^2 + 5x - 14 = 0.

questions.stem: What is the product of the roots of $4x^2 - 8x + 1 = 0$?
questions.explanation: The product of the roots is c/a = 1/4. The sum would be -b/a = 2, which is a different quantity.

questions.stem: Solve $x^2 + 4x + 1 = 0$, giving your answers in exact surd form.
questions.explanation: Discriminant = 16 - 4 = 12, so x = (-4 +/- sqrt(12))/2 = (-4 +/- 2 sqrt(3))/2 = -2 +/- sqrt(3). Option 2 forgets to divide the surd by 2 and to simplify sqrt(12).

questions.stem: Write $2x^2 + 4x - 3$ in the form $a(x + p)^2 + q$.
questions.explanation: Factor first: 2(x^2 + 2x) - 3 = 2[(x + 1)^2 - 1] - 3 = 2(x + 1)^2 - 2 - 3 = 2(x + 1)^2 - 5. The -3 alone (option 3) forgets to multiply the subtracted square by the outer 2.

questions.stem: The equation $kx^2 + 8x + 4 = 0$ has two equal roots. What is the value of $k$?
questions.explanation: Equal roots means the discriminant is zero: 64 - 16k = 0, so k = 4.

questions.stem: Which equation with integer coefficients has roots $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $-3$?
questions.explanation: Sum of roots = -5/2 and product = -3/2, giving x^2 + (5/2)x - 3/2 = 0; doubling every term gives 2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0. Check by factorising: (2x - 1)(x + 3).
